problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.3 \\ 1 & 0.7\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 2x2 Matrix
examples.problem:
The table below describes how the customers of a particular electronics store feel about their next computer purchase.

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Laptop** | **Desktop** |
| To: | **Laptop** | $0.9$ | $0.8$ |
| **Desktop** | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |  |

It is found that $10 \%$ of customers who currently use a laptop would choose a desktop on their next purchase, while $80 \%$ of customers who currently use a desktop would choose a laptop on their next purchase. 

Given that the store has $5\,400$ customers, all of whom purchase a new computer every two years, how many customers would eventually own a desktop computer if the given probabilities remain constant over many two-year periods?
examples.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14061943/assets/1935c4960a48e2b446c2610b9edc2a160a5f45462494c72a90f139ea2d13cc34.png)

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many two-year periods, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14061943/assets/29b5a209bb27b24f165ee418326763d8fb24f83f2b3a767052c381aa8cd0e01c.png)

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.8 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=8{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14061943/assets/0e8f620c3392dbb77b1353184e38eaf48b526aa82c502772a5582bd20c7f5aea.png)

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}8{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ 9{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Our steady-state vector is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14061943/assets/2ed7b0fc7296b2b651909c7c15c73e253fc8a9f95fb037072228d5de6f838894.png)

So, ${\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{9}}}$ of the $5\,400$ customers would eventually own a desktop computer. Therefore, the total number of people who would eventually own a desktop computer is

$$
\dfrac{1}{9} \cdot 5\,400 = 600.
$$

feedback.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.5 \\ 1 & 0.5\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the stochastic matrix $P$ and vector $q$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

- $q$ is a stochastic vector
- $Pq=q$
- $q$ is a steady-state vector of $P$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that $Pq=q.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $q$ is a stochastic vector since its entries are non-negative and add up to $1.$

- Statement II is false. Note that

$$
Pq=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.5 \\ 1 & 0.5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0+\frac{1.5}{4} \\ \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1.5}{4}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8} \\ \frac{5}{8}\end{aligned}]\ne q.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $Pq\ne q,$ it is not a steady-state vector of $P.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
